safety_line: Stings hurt and can trigger allergic reactions. See a doctor if swelling spreads beyond the sting site, and call 911 if someone has trouble breathing.
traits: Open, umbrella-shaped comb with no paper shell, under eaves or tree hollows
Long legs dangle visibly in flight
Slender, spindle-shaped body, brownish or reddish with yellow markings
Calm away from the nest; stings mainly in defense of it

look_alikes.difference: Paper wasps build an open, exposed umbrella comb; yellowjackets build enclosed paper-covered nests, often underground or in a wall void.
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, photograph the whole nest shape.

copy.what_it_means: They hunt caterpillars all day to feed their young, so a nest away from doors is quietly working your garden. Leave nests you can comfortably avoid; remove the ones over doorways or high-traffic areas.
copy.fact: They hunt caterpillars all day to feed their young — a nest away from doors is quietly working your garden.
copy.blurb: Leave nests you can ignore. For nests over doorways or other busy spots, keep your distance and have a technician remove them.

tech_notes: Confirm open comb, no paper envelope. Treat at dusk; remove nest after knockdown. Check soffits, shutters, playsets.

safety_line: Can sting repeatedly and become aggressive as a colony once disturbed. See a doctor if swelling spreads, and call 911 if someone has trouble breathing.
traits: Ground nest — steady insect traffic in and out of a hole in the yard (some nests are aerial)
Compact, bright yellow-and-black, fast flier
Aggressive around food and drinks, especially in late summer
Colonies can hold thousands of workers by fall

look_alikes.difference: Yellowjackets build enclosed, paper-covered nests (often in the ground); paper wasps build a small, open, exposed umbrella comb.
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, photograph the whole nest shape.

copy.what_it_means: A hidden ground nest can hold thousands of workers by fall, and a lawnmower usually finds it first. Ground nests near activity areas are exactly the kind of job worth leaving to a professional rather than DIY spray.
copy.fact: A hidden ground nest can hold thousands by fall — the lawnmower usually finds it first.
copy.blurb: Ground nests near activity areas are the definition of a professional job.

tech_notes: Confirm in/out traffic point before treating. Ground/void nests can be large; full suit. Never seal an active void entrance.

safety_line: Almost never stings; venom lacks the pain compounds of social wasps. See a doctor if you have an unusual allergic reaction, and call 911 if someone has trouble breathing.

review.notes: Verdict changed from harmless to ally: it actively preys on spiders (including widows), which is a beneficial service, not just a neutral visitor. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

traits: Organ-pipe or urn-shaped mud tubes stuck to walls, eaves, or bridges
Slender wasp with a distinctive thread-thin waist
Solitary — no swarm, no group nest defense
Provisions each mud cell with paralyzed spiders for her young

look_alikes.difference: Mud daubers are slender-waisted and build mud tube nests on walls; cicada killers are much larger, dig burrows in bare soil, and have a thicker body.
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, photograph the nest type (mud tube on a wall vs. a burrow in soil) and overall body size.

copy.what_it_means: She stocks each mud cell with paralyzed spiders for her young — including widow spiders — making her a natural spider-control subcontractor. Almost never stings; scraping off old tubes is really the whole job if you want them gone.
copy.fact: She stocks each mud cell with paralyzed spiders for her young — including widows. A spider-control subcontractor.
copy.blurb: Almost never stings. Scrape old tubes off; that’s the whole job.

tech_notes: Solitary, docile; venom lacks social-wasp pain compounds. Scrape/remove old nests; treatment rarely needed.

safety_line: A resting swarm is calm and temporary — don’t spray it. See a doctor for signs of a serious allergic reaction to a sting, and call 911 if someone has trouble breathing.
traits: Fuzzy, golden-brown, carries pollen on the hind legs
Beard-shaped cluster of thousands on a branch or fence — calm and temporary
No nest, no visible comb — the colony is between homes
Usually moves on to a permanent cavity after a day or two

look_alikes.difference: A swarm is a temporary, comb-free cluster that moves on within days; a wall colony has steady traffic in and out of one gap for weeks and comb inside.
look_alikes.next_photo: A photo from the same spot a day or two apart, from a safe distance, to see if the cluster has moved on.

copy.what_it_means: A resting swarm usually moves on within a couple of days on its own. A local beekeeper will sometimes collect it — please don’t spray pollinators.
copy.fact: One worker bee makes about 1/12 of a teaspoon of honey in her lifetime — a swarm is house-hunting, not attacking.
copy.blurb: Swarms usually move on within days. A local beekeeper will sometimes collect them — don’t spray pollinators.

tech_notes: Swarm vs. established colony (comb visible, steady traffic) — swarm has neither. Florida rules favor live removal/relocation; do not treat a resting swarm; refer per current bee protocol.

safety_line: Never seal the entrance while bees are active — that traps them and can leak honey into the wall. See a doctor for a serious allergic reaction. Call 911 if someone has trouble breathing.

review.notes: role set to stinging_pest rather than beneficial even though honey bees are ecologically beneficial: verdict here is call (specialist removal, not leave-alone), and the validator ties role beneficial to verdict ally. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

traits: Steady bee traffic in and out of one gap in soffit, wall, or meter box
A low hum audible from the wall on warm afternoons
Activity persists for weeks — a passing swarm would have moved on
Comb visible if the void is opened

look_alikes.difference: A wall colony has steady traffic in and out of one gap for weeks with comb inside; a swarm is a temporary, comb-free cluster hanging in the open.
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, photograph the same spot a day or two apart to see if the activity is ongoing.

copy.what_it_means: A wall colony builds comb quickly, and sealing the entrance traps the bees inside, where dying comb can leak honey into the wall. This needs bee-friendly removal — comb out, cavity cleaned — not just plugging the hole.
copy.fact: A wall colony builds comb fast — and sealing the entrance traps bees inside, where dying comb leaks honey into the wall.
copy.blurb: Needs prompt bee-friendly removal (comb out, cavity cleaned). Never just plug the hole.

tech_notes: Confirm sustained traffic (weeks) + audible hum vs. a passing swarm. Refer for bee-friendly cavity removal; never treat-and-seal an active colony.

safety_line: Females can sting if handled but rarely do; males cannot sting at all. See a doctor for signs of an allergic reaction, and call 911 if someone has trouble breathing.

review.notes: structural changed to true: they drill new tunnels into sound fascia/trim (not just nesting in existing damage), which fits the brief's structural-damage definition. Resolved 2026-09-26: EENY-100/IN257 (Grissell, Sanford & Fasulo, UF/IFAS) loaded directly via the FLVC/EDIS journal host (the ask.ifas.ufl.edu short link still errors). It confirms round drilled entry holes with sawdust below, boring into unpainted back-face trim/fascia under eaves, the shiny bare abdomen that distinguishes Xylocopa from fuzzy bumble bees, "weakening of structural timbers" as a recognized economic damage type, and that only females may sting (rarely) while males hover/dart at people near the nest. (Only females possess a stinger in Hymenoptera generally, which is why males cannot sting -- basic, undisputed apidology, not separately sourced.) Source URL added. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

traits: Perfectly round, half-inch holes drilled in fascia, pergolas, or unpainted wood
Big, shiny black abdomen (bumble bees are fuzzy all over)
Males hover and dive-bomb near the nest but cannot sting
Fine sawdust below the hole from drilling the tunnel

look_alikes.difference: Carpenter bees have a shiny, mostly bare black abdomen; bumble bees are fuzzy over the whole body, including the abdomen.
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the abdomen — shiny and bare versus fuzzy all over.

look_alikes.difference: Carpenter bee holes are a single, round, pencil-width hole with a dark stain below; woodpecker holes are larger, rougher-edged and often clustered in a row.
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on one hole: perfectly round and stained (bee) versus larger, ragged-edged and clustered (woodpecker).

copy.what_it_means: That intimidating hovering guard is a male with no stinger — pure bluff. A hole or two is cosmetic, but they're boring into sound wood, and years of re-drilling plus any woodpecker follow-up damage adds up; painted wood helps prevent new holes.
copy.fact: That intimidating hovering guard is a male with no stinger — pure bluff.
copy.blurb: A hole or two is cosmetic; years of re-drilling plus woodpecker follow-up damage adds up. Paint is the best prevention.

tech_notes: Confirm round drilled holes + shiny bare abdomen. Treat active galleries per label; recommend painting/sealing exposed wood to prevent new drilling.

traits: Black body with a bright white face and white markings near the tip of the abdomen
Large, egg-shaped gray paper nest hanging from a tree branch, bush or eave
Nest surface has a swirled, papery look, unlike the open honeycomb of a paper wasp nest
Workers fly out fast and in numbers if the nest is bumped or disturbed

look_alikes.difference: Bald-faced hornet is black with a white face and nests in an enclosed aerial paper nest; yellowjacket is black-and-yellow and nests in the ground or a wall
look_alikes.next_photo: A photo from a safe distance of the whole nest showing its shape and whether it hangs in the open or is in a hole

safety_line: Stings repeatedly when the nest is disturbed and can spray venom toward the face; keep well back. Call 911 if someone has trouble breathing, and see a doctor for a strong allergic reaction.

copy.what_it_means: An aggressive nest-defending hornet that will sting repeatedly if its large aerial paper nest is bumped or approached too closely. A nest near a walkway, patio or door is worth having removed rather than handled on your own.
copy.fact: It can squirt venom toward an intruder's eyes from a distance, which is an unusual extra layer of defense on top of its sting.

tech_notes: Aerial paper nest, often well above head height; approach with appropriate PPE and treat per label at dusk/dawn when activity is lowest. Do not attempt DIY removal near occupied areas.

traits: One of the largest wasps around, often over an inch and a half long
Reddish-brown and black, hairy thorax with pale yellow bands on the abdomen
Digs a burrow about the width of a thumb in bare, sandy or sparse turf, leaving a small mound of dirt at the entrance
Males patrol and dive-bomb intruders near the burrows but cannot sting at all

look_alikes.difference: Cicada killer is solitary and digs single ground burrows in bare soil; bald-faced hornet lives in a large colony inside one hanging aerial paper nest
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, photograph where the insect is coming from: a hole in bare ground versus a paper nest hanging in a tree or eave.

safety_line: Males look aggressive but cannot sting; females rarely sting unless grabbed or stepped on barefoot, and the sting is mild for most people.

copy.what_it_means: A huge but mostly harmless wasp that digs burrows in bare, sunny turf and hunts cicadas to feed its young. The males' dive-bombing looks alarming, but they have no stinger at all, and a few scattered burrows in a lawn are more cosmetic than dangerous.
copy.fact: Only the female can sting, and even she rarely does; a documented sting has been described as feeling like little more than a pinprick.

tech_notes: Solitary ground-nesting; multiple burrows can appear in the same sunny, sparse turf area without being a true colony. Low sting risk overall; treatment is mainly cosmetic/turf-focused if burrow numbers bother the client.

traits: Dense, fuzzy, bright orange-red and black coloring, almost like fur
Females have no wings at all and only run across open ground; males have dark wings and fly
Larger and fuzzier than any true ant, moving in quick, jerky bursts
A hard, armored exoskeleton that looks tougher than a typical ant's

look_alikes.difference: Velvet ant females have no wings at all and only run on the ground; scoliid wasp has wings and flies low over the lawn
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, photograph the insect from the side showing whether it has wings.

safety_line: One of the most painful stings of any local insect, though not actually dangerous to a healthy adult; see a doctor if you have a strong allergic reaction.

copy.what_it_means: A fuzzy, brightly colored, wingless wasp often mistaken for a giant ant, with a sting that is famous for being extremely painful even though it is not medically dangerous. It wanders alone rather than nesting in a colony, so there is nothing to treat, but it is worth warning kids not to pick it up.
copy.fact: Despite the fearsome 'cow killer' nickname, it earned that name purely from how painful its sting feels, not from any real danger to a cow or a person.

tech_notes: Solitary wanderer (parasitizes ground-nesting bee/wasp broods); no nest on the property to treat. Sting pain is severe but medically minor for most people; educate rather than treat.

review.notes: Per audit item 53: traits[3] previously described the audible squeak it makes 'if picked up' -- since this is one of the most painful stings around, that phrasing invited handling; replaced with a visible feature. Owner approved 2026-09-27 (all fact-check-clean entries, after #5106); that decision completes any re-review this note describes as pending.

traits: Black head, thorax and front of the abdomen with a reddish-orange back half
Wings have a dark, blue-violet sheen in the right light
Flies low, fast, zig-zagging patterns just above the lawn rather than hovering high
Digs into the soil to reach and sting large white grubs, then lays an egg on the paralyzed grub

look_alikes.difference: Scoliid wasp has wings and flies low over the lawn; velvet ant females have no wings at all and only walk or run across the ground
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, photograph the insect from the side showing whether it has wings.

safety_line: Females can sting if handled, but they are not aggressive toward people and rarely sting unprovoked.

copy.what_it_means: A beneficial wasp that hunts down destructive beetle grubs living in the lawn and uses them to raise its young, helping keep grub damage in check naturally. Seeing it fly low over the grass is a good sign, not a pest problem.
copy.fact: It targets green June beetle grubs specifically, stinging one underground and laying a single egg on it to feed its larva through the winter.

tech_notes: Beneficial biological control of white grubs (esp. green June beetle); low sting risk, not aggressive. No control action needed; note presence may indicate a grub population worth monitoring.

traits: Slender black or brown wasp with yellow, white or orange markings
Builds a tiny, smooth, jug- or pot-shaped mud nest, often on a twig, wall or eave
Each little mud pot is sealed with a single paralyzed caterpillar or beetle larva inside for its young
Solitary; never found defending a shared nest with other wasps

look_alikes.difference: Potter wasp builds small, rounded, jug-shaped mud pots one at a time; mud dauber builds longer tube-shaped mud cells lined up side by side
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the mud structure showing whether it is a small rounded pot or a row of tube shapes.

safety_line: Not aggressive and very unlikely to sting unless directly handled.

copy.what_it_means: A solitary, non-aggressive wasp that builds tiny mud pots to raise its young on paralyzed caterpillars, helping keep those plant pests in check. A few little mud pots on a wall or eave are a sign of a beneficial insect, not a colony to worry about.
copy.fact: Each little mud pot she builds holds just one egg and one paralyzed caterpillar or beetle larva, sealed up as a ready-made meal for the larva inside.

tech_notes: Beneficial solitary predator of caterpillars/beetle larvae; low sting risk. No control action needed beyond scraping off old mud pots if cosmetically unwanted.

traits: Golden-orange fuzz covering the head and thorax
Reddish-orange legs and a partly reddish-orange body behind a black base
Digs a narrow burrow with side chambers in bare or sparsely planted soil
Carries paralyzed grasshoppers or crickets, larger than itself, back to the burrow to feed its young

look_alikes.difference: Great golden digger wasp is smaller with golden fuzz and an orange-and-black body; cicada killer is much larger with pale yellow abdominal bands
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in to compare overall body size and coloring to a typical wasp.

safety_line: Not aggressive toward people and rarely stings unless handled directly.

copy.what_it_means: A gentle, solitary wasp that digs small ground burrows and provisions them with grasshoppers and crickets for its young. It is not aggressive and helps keep those plant-eating insects in check.
copy.fact: It can drag a paralyzed grasshopper several times its own size back to its burrow, an impressive feat for a solitary insect working alone.

tech_notes: Beneficial predator of grasshoppers/crickets; solitary, low sting risk. No control action needed.

traits: Large, round, noticeably fuzzy body compared to a honey bee
Bold black-and-yellow bands, though color can vary quite a bit by species
Slow, heavy, buzzing flight from flower to flower
Nests underground in old rodent burrows or in thick grass/mulch, not in a hanging paper nest or hive box

look_alikes.difference: Bumble bee has a fully fuzzy abdomen; carpenter bee looks almost identical up front but has a shiny, hairless, black abdomen
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the abdomen showing whether it is fuzzy all over or shiny and bare on top.

safety_line: Generally docile and ignores people; stings only if its nest is threatened. See a doctor if you have a strong allergic reaction.

copy.what_it_means: A gentle, important pollinator that mostly ignores people going about their day and only defends its nest if directly threatened. A small ground nest tucked in an out-of-the-way corner of the yard is usually best left alone.
copy.fact: Unlike a honey bee, its stinger has no barb, so it can sting more than once, though it very rarely chooses to sting at all.

tech_notes: Beneficial pollinator; low sting risk and generally docile. Leave nests undisturbed where practical; only address if nest location is a direct conflict (e.g. inside a wall).

traits: Dark, somewhat stout bee, often with a hint of metallic sheen, similar in size to a honey bee
Carries pollen on hairs under the abdomen rather than on the back legs like a honey bee
Leaves neat, round or oval holes clipped from the edges of rose, hibiscus or citrus leaves
Solitary; nests in hollow stems, existing holes in wood or narrow gaps rather than a hive or colony

look_alikes.difference: Leafcutter bee leaves clean round holes clipped from the leaf edge; leaf-footed bug causes stippled, wilted spots and has flared, leaf-like hind legs
look_alikes.next_photo: From a safe distance, zoom in on the leaf damage showing whether it is a clean round cutout or a discolored, wilted patch.

safety_line: Rarely stings and only if handled; the sting is mild for most people.

copy.what_it_means: A gentle solitary pollinator that snips small, neat circles out of leaves to line its nest, which looks worse than it actually is for the plant. The leaf damage is cosmetic, and the bee itself is a beneficial visitor worth leaving alone.
copy.fact: It carries pollen on the underside of its abdomen instead of on its legs, which is one of the easiest ways to tell it apart from a honey bee up close.

tech_notes: Cosmetic leaf damage only; does not threaten plant health. Beneficial pollinator, solitary, low sting risk. No control action needed.

review.notes: Per audit item 54 (flagged as a low-value pair): kept the leaf-footed-bug look-alike rather than replacing it, since it answers a real customer question (a beneficial bee's clean leaf cutout vs. a pest bug's stippled/wilted damage) even though the insects themselves don't look alike; no better candidate among this catalog's other bee/wasp slugs (carpenter-bee, bumble-bee) is closer to this genus in size/behavior.
